The concrete server configuration uses the RHEL 9 family. Ubuntu differences are identified where they change a path, package, account group, or security mechanism. Do not combine both distributions’ instructions on one host.

slides.title: 33.1 Requirements
keyPoints: Linux example — 33.1
Capture a baseline alongside the service requirements.
What to check: Translate capacity, access, availability, and recovery requirements into acceptance tests.
slides.narration:
Write the acceptance contract before installing anything. For this lab, the site must return the approved release marker at https://status.harbor.test/index.html, authenticate the server with a certificate that the test client explicitly trusts, allow administration through a verified named account, and prevent the web worker from modifying the deployed content. Logging, a bounded external check, a recoverable backup, and a tested rebuild procedure are required.

The teaching recovery objectives are a recovery point no older than 24 hours and recovery within 60 minutes of declaring a restore. These are exercises, not promises about an untested design. Decide what starts and stops each clock. A single web server has a single-server failure domain; nothing in this chapter turns it into a highly available service.

Record the service owner, approved client network, administrative source, data classification, expected requests, patch window, certificate owner, and alert recipient. Unknown values are unresolved requirements. An invented IP address in a worksheet is not authorization to use it on a real network.

slides.title: 33.3 Storage Layout
keyPoints: Linux example — 33.3
Inspect storage layout and mount policy.
What to check: Confirm capacity and intended persistence before deploying application data.
slides.narration:
For a small teaching VM, the operating system and site can share the system filesystem. Document the consequence: log growth and application data compete with the operating system for capacity. A separate data volume can isolate capacity and simplify certain recovery operations, but it also adds a required mount and its own failure cases. Choose deliberately rather than treating a diagram’s extra disks as automatic reliability.

Use /srv/harbor/site for deployed content and /var/log/nginx for service logs. Record the filesystem type, size, persistent identifier, mount options, free-block threshold, and free-inode threshold. Verify any required data mount before deployment; otherwise a missing mount can leave a deceptively writable directory on the root filesystem.

findmnt --target /srv identifies the filesystem containing that path. Compare its reported target and source with the design; it does not by itself prove that /srv is a separate mount. Do not partition or format the installed system disk during this capstone. Use Chapters 9 and 10 for separately identified disposable storage exercises.

slides.title: 33.4 Network Configuration
keyPoints: Linux example — 33.4
Inspect addressing, routes, and resolution.
What to check: The capstone name must resolve through the intended client path, not only a temporary override.
slides.narration:
Assign web1 an address that the isolated lab actually permits. This chapter continues the example address 192.168.56.20, but the address must be replaced when the lab differs. Verify the interface, connection profile, prefix, gateway, and resolver owner before changing persistent configuration. Apply remote network changes only with working console recovery.

Use the persistent NetworkManager procedure from Chapter 11 rather than adding a temporary address and assuming it will survive reboot. Register the name through the lab’s DNS service, or use a deliberate client /etc/hosts entry for the isolated exercise. Record which approach was used. A later curl --resolve test intentionally bypasses DNS, so it cannot substitute for a separate normal-name lookup test.

Decide whether the service supports IPv6. Configure and test its address, listener, routing, and firewall policy when it does. The IPv4-only examples below do not silently provide an IPv6 service or establish an IPv6 security policy. (R27, R31)

keyPoints: Linux example — 33.12
Run independent state, resource, and client probes.
What to check: The regular HTTPS probe requires configured trust and DNS; preserve any failure instead of disabling validation.
slides.narration:
Measure both the host and the user-facing service. Host checks cover storage space, inodes, memory pressure, service state, time synchronization, and required mount availability. slides.title: 33.14 Automated Patching
keyPoints: Linux example — 33.14
Inspect patch schedules without enabling a new one.
What to check: Confirm repository scope, reboot policy, monitoring, and maintenance ownership before activation.
slides.narration:
Automate observation before automating uncontrolled change. For the RHEL 9-family exercise, DNF Automatic can notify, download, or install according to the selected service and timer. Inspect the installed package’s configuration and timer files before enabling a schedule. Function-specific timers can override the download/apply behavior in the configuration.

A cautious initial exercise uses the installed dnf-automatic-download.timer, when provided, to stage updates without installing them. A security-only selection depends on available repository advisory metadata; an empty selection does not prove that every package is secure. Decide when ordinary bug-fix updates also belong in the baseline.

Move to automatic installation only after establishing maintenance behavior, restart or reboot handling, a canary, rollback or rebuild, and the external acceptance check. Ubuntu’s unattended-upgrades workflow needs the same operational decisions but different configuration. Reconcile the running kernel and restarted services after patching rather than recording only the transaction’s exit status. (R69, R12, R13)

keyPoints: Linux example — 33.16
Collect baseline evidence before controlled failure injection.
What to check: Break only the isolated lab using the chapter's specific scenario and preserve console access and rollback.
slides.narration:
Test controlled failures in the isolated lab with console access and a saved baseline. Stop the service, publish a deliberately different release marker, and introduce a candidate configuration syntax error without replacing the active valid configuration. Each case should produce the expected failed acceptance check and a distinct diagnostic path.

Test certificate rejection using a wrong service name or an untrusted test certificate on a separate fixture. Preserve the trusted site’s configuration. For storage and permission failures, use the bounded exercises in Chapter 32; do not fill the system disk or exhaust host memory just to obtain a dramatic screenshot.

For every injected fault, record the expected signal, actual observation, detection delay, recovery action, and restored acceptance result. Restore the baseline before starting the next fault so one unresolved problem does not contaminate the next experiment. Failed or missing detections become work items, not suppressed alerts.

Review area | Evidence required before approval
Service contract | Correct named HTTPS response and exact release marker from the intended client path
Administration | Fresh approved login, tested elevation, and protected console recovery
Storage and access | Verified mounts, capacity thresholds, ownership, and mandatory-access-control state
Operations | Delivered test alert, usable logs, defined patch/restart process, and assigned owners
Recovery | Independent backup restored onto a separate host within the declared objectives
Security | Allowed and rejected paths tested; key access and relevant exceptions reviewed
Change and handover | Versioned configuration, rollback evidence, and an independently usable runbook

A single-server lab may be adequate for a low-criticality internal exercise while failing a requirement for continuous availability. The answer depends on the contract, not on how many commands were entered.
